title: Convert Binary Search Tree to Sorted Doubly Linked List
description: Brute force to optimized: collecting sorted values into an array versus re-linking BST nodes directly during a single in-order traversal.

sections.title: Convert Binary Search Tree to Sorted Doubly Linked List

content.title: Convert Binary Search Tree to Sorted Doubly Linked List

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Given the root of a Binary Search Tree, convert it to a sorted CIRCULAR doubly linked list in place, reusing the tree's existing nodes: each node's "left" pointer becomes the "previous" pointer, and its "right" pointer becomes the "next" pointer. Return a pointer to the smallest element.

blocks.caption: An in-order traversal of a BST visits nodes in sorted order; linking each node to the previously-visited one builds the sorted doubly linked list directly

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","The root of a Binary Search Tree"],["Output","A pointer to the smallest node, now part of a sorted CIRCULAR doubly linked list (using the same left/right pointers as previous/next)"],["Goal","Convert the tree in place, reusing existing nodes, without creating any new nodes"],["Constraints","The number of nodes is in the range [0, 2000]; -1000 <= Node.val <= 1000; all values are unique"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["A BST needs to become SORTED linear order","An in-order traversal, since it visits a BST's nodes in exactly ascending sorted order by definition"],["The result must be a CIRCULAR doubly linked list, reusing the same node pointers (left=prev, right=next)","Track the \"previously visited\" node during the in-order traversal, linking it forward/backward to each newly visited node as the traversal proceeds"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

A Binary Search Tree's in-order traversal visits values in ascending sorted order; this problem asks to physically RE-LINK the tree's own nodes (reinterpreting left/right as prev/next) into that same sorted order, forming a doubly linked list that is also CIRCULAR (the last node connects back to the first).

blocks.title: Analogy: Turning a Family Tree Into a Single-File Line, Sorted by Age, in a Loop
blocks.text: Imagine a family tree structure where visiting it in a specific "in-order" way naturally lists everyone from youngest to oldest. This problem asks to physically rearrange everyone's "points to" relationships (previously representing family connections) into a single-file line ordered by age, where each person points forward to the next-oldest and backward to the next-youngest, and cleverly, the oldest person also loops back around to point forward to the youngest, forming a closed loop.

blocks.caption: Tracking the most recently visited node during an in-order traversal lets each new node be linked directly to it, one connection at a time

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: BST with root 4, left subtree rooted at 2 (children 1 and 3), right child 5

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["In-order traversal visits: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5","Sorted order confirmed","Standard BST in-order property"],["Link each node to the previously visited one as it is reached: 1<->2<->3<->4<->5","A sorted doubly linked list (not yet circular)","Each new node is linked forward from, and backward to, the previously visited node"],["Close the circle: 5 (the last/largest) connects forward to 1 (the first/smallest), and 1 connects backward to 5","A sorted CIRCULAR doubly linked list","The defining \"circular\" requirement of this specific problem"],["Answer","Circular DLL: 1<->2<->3<->4<->5<->(back to 1)","The smallest node (1) is returned as the result"]]}

blocks.text: Example: A single-node tree (just the root)

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["The single node is its own predecessor and successor","A circular list of size 1 (the node points to itself in both directions)","Closing the circle with only one node means it wraps back to itself"]]}

blocks.text: 5. How Should We Think?

Before extracting values into a sorted array and rebuilding an entirely new doubly linked list, notice that the BST's OWN in-order traversal already visits nodes in sorted order, so the existing nodes can simply be re-linked as they are visited.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: An in-order traversal (left subtree, current node, right subtree) of a BST is GUARANTEED to visit nodes in ascending sorted order, by the BST property itself.

Observation 2: Tracking a "last visited node" variable throughout the traversal means that, at each newly visited node, its predecessor (the previous sorted value) is already known and can be linked immediately: last.right = current, current.left = last.

Observation 3: The very FIRST node visited has no predecessor yet, so it must be specially remembered as the eventual head of the result (rather than linked to anything at that point).

Observation 4: After the traversal completes, "last" holds the LARGEST value's node (the traversal's final visit), which needs one final pair of links to the remembered first node, closing the circle.

Recognizing that re-linking can happen DURING the same in-order traversal (rather than as a separate pass after collecting values) avoids any extra O(n) array entirely.

This is an in-order traversal that re-links nodes AS they are visited, tracking the previously-visited node throughout, then closing the circle with one final pair of links after the traversal completes.
6. Brute Force Solution
Perform a standard in-order traversal, collecting values into a sorted array (this is simply the BST property applied directly), representing the "flattened" sorted sequence.
Step by step algorithm

items: Perform a standard in-order traversal (left, current, right), appending each node's value to a result array as it is visited.
The resulting array is already in ascending sorted order, by the BST's in-order property.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Collecting values via an in-order traversal (or equivalently, being handed the already-sorted values) directly reflects the BST's inherent sorted structure.
This representation captures the CORRECT final order, but does not actually produce the required re-linked circular doubly linked list structure using the tree's own nodes.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Correctly identifies the sorted order of values, since in-order traversal is guaranteed to visit a BST in ascending order.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single traversal.
Space: O(n) for the array, plus O(h) recursion stack (h = tree height).

Limitation: collecting into a separate array does not perform the required IN-PLACE re-linking of the tree's own nodes; re-linking during the SAME in-order traversal achieves the actual required result directly.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force only collects sorted VALUES, not an actual re-linked structure. Instead, perform the SAME in-order traversal, but at each node visited, immediately link it to the previously-visited node (tracked in a "last" variable): last.right = current, current.left = last. The very first node visited is remembered separately (no predecessor exists yet). After the traversal, one final pair of links between the remembered first node and the final "last" node closes the circle.

Maintain first and last as shared state across the traversal (both initially null/None). In the in-order traversal: recurse left, then if last exists link last.right = node and node.left = last, else set first = node; update last = node; then recurse right. After the full traversal: link last.right = first and first.left = last, and return first.
9. Optimized Solution
Perform an in-order traversal, re-linking each node to the previously-visited one as it is reached, then close the circle after the traversal completes.
Dry run for BST with root 4, left subtree rooted at 2 (children 1, 3), right child 5

blocks.content: {"headers":["Visit order","Node","Action"],"rows":[["1st","1","last is null: first = node(1); last = node(1)"],["2nd","2","last(1).right = node(2); node(2).left = last(1); last = node(2)"],["3rd","3","last(2).right = node(3); node(3).left = last(2); last = node(3)"],["4th","4","last(3).right = node(4); node(4).left = last(3); last = node(4)"],["5th","5","last(4).right = node(5); node(5).left = last(4); last = node(5)"],["After traversal","-","last(5).right = first(1); first(1).left = last(5): circle closed"]]}

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: The result is a circular doubly linked list 1<->2<->3<->4<->5<->(back to 1), with first (value 1) returned as the head, matching the expected result.

codes.python:
def tree_to_doubly_list(root):
    if not root:
        return None

    first = [None]                                                          # boxed in a list so the nested function can mutate it
    last = [None]

    def inorder(node):
        if not node:
            return
        inorder(node.left)                                                  # visit the left subtree FIRST (smaller values)
        if last[0]:
            last[0].right = node                                           # link the PREVIOUSLY visited node forward to this one
            node.left = last[0]                                            # and this one backward to it
        else:
            first[0] = node                                                # the very first node visited becomes the list's head
        last[0] = node
        inorder(node.right)                                                 # visit the right subtree LAST (larger values)

    inorder(root)
    last[0].right = first[0]                                                # close the circle: tail connects forward to head
    first[0].left = last[0]                                                 # and head connects backward to tail
    return first[0]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    n1, n3, n5 = TreeNode(1), TreeNode(3), TreeNode(5)
    n2 = TreeNode(2, n1, n3)
    root = TreeNode(4, n2, n5)
    head = tree_to_doubly_list(root)
    values = []
    node = head
    for _ in range(5):
        values.append(node.val)
        node = node.right
    print(values)

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single in-order traversal.
Space: O(h) recursion stack (h = tree height); O(1) additional beyond that, since existing nodes are reused.
Why This Works

Since in-order traversal is guaranteed to visit BST nodes in ascending sorted order, linking each newly visited node to whatever was visited immediately before it (tracked via "last") directly builds the correctly sorted doubly linked list, one connection at a time, with zero extra nodes created. The very first node visited (the overall smallest value) has no predecessor during the traversal itself, so it is remembered separately and only linked at the very END, when closing the circle with the last (largest) node.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["The first node visited (smallest value)","No \"last\" exists yet, so it is remembered as \"first\" instead of being linked"],["Every subsequent node visited","Immediately linked to \"last\" (the previously visited node) in both directions"],["After the full traversal completes","A final pair of links between \"first\" and \"last\" closes the circle"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: first and last are maintained as shared state across the recursive traversal (module/class-level variables, or boxed values, depending on the language), since a single traversal function alone cannot easily return two separate pieces of running state.
The in-order recursion order (left, process current, right) is exactly what guarantees nodes are visited, and thus linked, in ascending sorted order.

The final circle-closing step (last.right = first, first.left = last) must happen strictly AFTER the traversal completes, since "last" only holds its final (largest-value) value once every node has been visited.

blocks.text: 10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space","Notes"],"rows":[["Brute force (in-order collect into a sorted array)","O(n)","O(n) + O(h) recursion","Correctly identifies sorted order, but does not produce the required re-linked structure"],["Optimized (re-link during the same in-order traversal)","O(n)","O(h) recursion, O(1) additional","Directly builds the required circular doubly linked list using the tree's own nodes"]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

Converting a BST into a sorted (doubly) linked list is a direct application of in-order traversal, since that traversal order IS the sorted order; re-linking nodes AS they are visited (tracking the previously-visited node) avoids any need for a separate collect-then-rebuild pass.
Common mistakes

items: Forgetting to specially remember the very FIRST node visited, since it has no predecessor to link to at the time it is visited.
Closing the circle (linking last to first) too early, before the traversal has actually reached the final (largest-value) node.
Confusing in-order traversal's recursion structure (left, current, right) with pre-order or post-order, which would NOT visit nodes in sorted order.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["Empty tree (root is null)","Return null directly, nothing to convert"],["A single-node tree","That single node becomes a circular list of size 1, pointing to itself in both directions"],["A completely skewed tree (e.g., every node has only a right child)","Still correctly handled, since in-order traversal order depends only on BST structure, not balance"]]}

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: Explicitly stating "in-order traversal visits a BST in sorted order, so this is really about re-linking DURING that traversal, not after" demonstrates the key insight clearly and concisely.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Convert a BST to a SORTED (doubly) linked list" points directly toward in-order traversal, since that traversal order inherently matches the required sorted order.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: Why must the result be CIRCULAR here specifically, and how does that change the algorithm? An extra final step (after the traversal) links the last node back to the first, which a simple (non-circular) conversion would omit entirely.
How would you convert to a NON-circular sorted doubly linked list instead? Skip the final circle-closing step; the rest of the in-order re-linking logic stays identical.

Could this be done iteratively instead of recursively? Yes, using an explicit stack to simulate the in-order traversal, tracking the "last visited node" exactly the same way, avoiding recursion stack space for very deep trees.

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: A direct application of BST in-order traversal (a fundamental tree technique) combined with the "track the previously visited node" linked-list re-linking style used throughout this category.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n) time, O(n) + O(h) space.
Optimized (re-link during the same in-order traversal): O(n) time, O(h) space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: In-order traversal with re-linking during the traversal

Core Idea: Track the previously-visited node throughout an in-order traversal, linking each new node to it immediately; remember the first node specially, and close the circle with one final pair of links after the traversal completes
Time: O(n)
Space: O(h) recursion stack
Most Important Observation: In-order traversal already visits BST nodes in exactly the required sorted order, so re-linking DURING that same traversal avoids any separate collect-then-rebuild pass
Interview Difficulty: Hard
One-line memory trick: In-order traversal; link last.right/node.left as you go; close the circle (last<->first) at the very end
